reviews.tradable-permits-and-carbon-markets: Every scheme in this chapter starts from one move: cap a pollutant, issue permits, and let trading put the cheapest cuts first. The Acid Rain Program proved the idea in the United States, and the EU Emissions Trading System and China's national scheme carried it to carbon. Their records show which design choices matter: free permits or auctions, too many permits or too few, and price limits such as the safety valve. Critics answer that trading can push emissions abroad, leave pollution near poor communities and reward gaming of credits. Meanwhile the same logic has spread beyond carbon, to water rights, energy savings, renewable power and building rights.

nature-pol-246.title: Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters
nature-pol-246.text: Grandfathering gives out emission permits for free, according to how much each firm emitted in the past. It can create perverse incentives. A firm that cuts its emissions sharply may receive fewer permits later. Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits. The EU's trading scheme gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition. Free allocation is complex, and it encourages lobbying and {{ref:nature-pol-042}}, the pursuit of favors from government.

nature-pol-248.title: Too many permits: how a carbon price collapses
nature-pol-248.text: A permit market lives or dies by the number of permits. Issue too many and the price sinks so low that firms have little reason to cut emissions. Issue too few and the risk flips to an excessively high price. Europe's trading scheme showed the first danger. Its price was fairly strong from 2005 to 2009 but was later undermined by oversupply and the Great Recession. Under the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}, Russia held surplus allowances after its economic collapse. Buying them would not have reduced emissions.

nature-pol-269.title: Certified emission reductions: credits from developing countries
nature-pol-269.text: Between 2001 and 7 September 2012, the {{ref:nature-mkt-104}} issued 1 billion certified emission reductions, or CERs. Each unit equals a cut of one tonne of {{ref:nature-eco-160}} (CO2e), measured against a baseline. Annex I countries buy them from projects in developing countries, where cuts are cheapest, and can use them to meet their Kyoto targets. By 2013, 57% came from destroying just two gases, HFC-23 or N2O. Prices fell from $20 a tonne in August 2008 to below $5 by September 2012, amid recession and over-allocation in Europe's trading scheme.

nature-pol-241.title: Carbon revenue: what to do with the money
nature-pol-241.text: A carbon tax or a permit auction raises money, and governments must decide how to spend it. One standard proposal returns it to the public per person. Richer people with bigger carbon footprints pay more, so poorer people can come out ahead. Per-person refunds would not, however, cover commuters in rural areas or people in poorly insulated houses. Other proposals fund renewable energy support, research, public transport and car sharing. Revenue could also pay for negative emissions, which remove carbon dioxide and cost about $150–165 per ton depending on the technology.

nature-pol-242.title: Why renewable energy support adds nothing under a binding cap
nature-pol-242.text: Under a carbon tax, public support for renewable energy adds to the emission cuts. Under a binding cap, it does not. While the cap applies, renewable support brings no further emission cuts, because the cap has already fixed the total amount emitted. So the choice between a tax and a cap ({{ref:nature-pol-240}}) also decides what other climate policies can achieve.

nature-pol-266.title: Assigned amount units: Kyoto's national allowances
nature-pol-266.text: Under the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}, each Annex 1 country received assigned amount units up to its emission target for the 2008–2012 commitment period. Each unit allowed it to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. Under Article 17, countries below their targets could sell spare units to countries above theirs. Such trading had to be supplemental to domestic action: a top-up to cuts at home, not a replacement.

nature-pol-271.title: Emission reduction units: credits from Joint Implementation
nature-pol-271.text: A landfill releases methane, a gas with a 100-year {{ref:nature-eco-159}} of 25 compared with carbon dioxide. Capture and burn one tonne of it, and it yields nearly 3 tonnes of CO2, a saving of 22 emission reduction units. Each unit is a Kyoto credit for one tonne of CO2 equivalent cut by a Joint Implementation project. The market for them later collapsed. ERU prices declined 89 percent in 2012, falling to 15 euro cents in December.

nature-pol-274.title: EU ETS2: a carbon market for buildings and road transport
nature-pol-274.text: EU ETS2 is a second European trading system for carbon dioxide from buildings, road transport and other sectors outside the original scheme. It covers emissions upstream: fuel suppliers, not end consumers, must report and pay for them. Its cap aims for a 42% cut by 2030 compared with 2005. Part of the revenue funds a Social Climate Fund for vulnerable groups. Together the two systems will cover 75% of EU greenhouse gas emissions. In 2025, under pressure from member states worried about inflation and energy affordability, its start was delayed to 2028.

nature-pol-273.title: The Market Stability Reserve: soaking up surplus permits
nature-pol-273.text: The Market Stability Reserve changes how many EU permits are auctioned each year, according to how many surplus permits are in circulation. It runs on predefined rules, with no discretion for the Commission or member states. It did not work at first. Back-loading and the reserve law failed to cut the surplus or lift prices in 2014–2017, when prices stayed below €10/tCO2. Since 2023, allowances in the reserve above a threshold are permanently invalidated. About 2.5 billion were invalidated on 1 January 2023.

nature-pol-264.title: Water trading: markets for the right to use water
nature-pol-264.text: Chile's 1981 Water Code made water rights freely tradable private property, a strongly free-market approach that has been controversial. Water trading is the buying and selling of water access entitlements, often called water rights, between willing sellers and buyers. A seller holds rights beyond its current needs, while a buyer short of water is willing to pay for more. Economic theory says trading moves water from less to more productive uses: urban users can pay up to 10 times more than farmers. The older first-in-time system of prior appropriation led to inefficient allocation and less adoption of water-saving technology. Water is a {{ref:nature-econ-610}}, but once rights make its use rival and excludable, it behaves like a private good. It is still no standard commodity. Supply is uncertain and moves through complex systems, and supply swings can leave markets thin. Trades can also harm or help third parties who are neither buyer nor seller. Schemes exist in the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Australia and elsewhere; some consider Australia's the most sophisticated.

nature-pol-267.title: CORSIA: offsetting the growth of international flights
nature-pol-267.text: In October 2016 the International Civil Aviation Organization adopted CORSIA, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation. It makes airlines buy credits ({{ref:nature-mkt-081}}) to offset growth in emissions from international flights, aiming for carbon-neutral growth from 2020. It is voluntary from 2021 until 2027, when it becomes compulsory, though least developed and small island states are not required to join. Domestic flights are not included, and it will regulate 25% of aviation's international emissions. Supporters call it a compromise step forward. Critics say it won't reduce jet fuel demand, and one hundred organizations rejected it as letting warming pass 1.5 °C.

nature-pol-279.title: Personal carbon trading: an allowance for every adult
nature-pol-279.text: Personal carbon trading would give each adult an equal share of emission credits within a national limit on emissions. People would surrender credits when buying fuel or electricity. Those who emit more than their allowance would buy credits from those who use less, who would profit. Research finds it would be progressive, moving money from rich to poor, unlike a carbon tax before its revenue is redistributed. Norfolk Island trialed the world's first program starting in 2011. Proponents call it fair and effective. Critics point to complexity, high costs and possible political unacceptability, and a 2008 UK study found it ahead of its time.

nature-pol-278.title: Market design: engineering the rules of exchange
nature-pol-278.text: Some markets are built on purpose. Market design is the branch of economics that sets the rules of exchange, who gets what and by what procedure, to build or repair markets so that they give efficient and fair outcomes. It is closely related to {{ref:nature-econ-008}} and auction theory. Alvin Roth pioneered applications in labor-market matching, organ transplantation and school choice. He and Shapley won the 2012 Nobel prize for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design. Auction theory supplies results such as the {{ref:nature-econ-009}}: with independent private values, sealed first-price and second-price auctions bring the same expected revenue.

nature-pol-283.title: Voluntary emission reductions: offsets bought by choice
nature-pol-283.text: Not every carbon offset is bought to meet a legal target. A Voluntary Emission Reduction, also called a Verified Emission Reduction or VER, is traded in the voluntary market. Companies and individuals buy them to compensate voluntarily for their emissions. They are usually certified outside the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. One VER equals 1 tonne of CO2 emissions. Standards set how reductions are measured, and every VER should at least be verified by an independent third party.

nature-pol-285.title: Windfall gains: income that drops from the sky
nature-pol-285.text: A windfall gain is a sudden, usually unexpected addition to {{ref:nature-econ-491}} well above the norm. It comes from luck or circumstance rather than planning. A windfall profit is the business version, caused for example by unexpected demand or by government regulation. Europe's carbon market supplied a case: fossil fuel generators priced freely allocated permits into electricity and reaped a massive windfall gain. Some legislators favor a windfall profits tax, since taxing unforeseen profits should not hurt the company.

nature-pol-263.title: Cap and dividend: sell the permits, pay the citizens
nature-pol-263.text: Who owns the sky? Peter Barnes asked in the title of his 2001 book, Who Owns the Sky?, where he first proposed the idea as 'Skytrust'. Cap and dividend is a cap-and-trade system in which all permits are sold and the money is paid back to citizens to offset higher energy prices. The cap often falls on upstream sources such as fossil fuel suppliers, which must buy permits for their emissions. Unlike ordinary cap and trade, no permits are given away free. The pollution rents, the value of the scarce permits, are captured publicly rather than becoming private assets. Households that emit least receive a bigger dividend than they pay in higher prices, which rewards those who conserve. A 2009 US bill would have auctioned 100 percent of permits and returned all proceeds as a monthly dividend, but it did not pass. The policy was vigorously debated: one critic called it 'fatally incomplete', while Time magazine hailed it.

nature-pol-276.title: Green certificates: trading proof of renewable power
nature-pol-276.text: A green certificate proves that a certain amount of electricity, typically one megawatthour, came from renewable sources. It represents the environmental value of that power and can be traded separately from the electricity itself. Poland, Sweden, the UK, Italy and Belgium use such certificates as a more market-like alternative to {{ref:nature-pol-224}}. There is a catch. Buying a certificate only shifts the claim to renewable power; it does not change how much renewable energy is generated.

nature-pol-286.title: Pollution hot spots: when location matters
nature-pol-286.text: Carbon dioxide has a similar effect wherever it is released, so for trading its location does not matter. Regional pollutants such as SO2, NOx and mercury are different. The same amount does far more harm in some places than in others, so under a cap it can pile up in hot spots. Carbon trading has a related blind spot. Because it limits only greenhouse gases, factories can buy permits without cutting local air pollution, leaving nearby low-income communities exposed. One answer is markets in location-based pollution licenses, which cap the rise in pollution at each monitoring point ({{ref:nature-pol-260}}).

nature-pol-260.title: Ambient permits: trading the right to raise local pollution
nature-pol-260.text: An ordinary permit grants the right to emit a set amount. An ambient permit grants the right to raise pollution at a given location by no more than a set amount. Pollution at each monitoring point is modeled as a weighted sum of all emissions, written q=H⋅e, where the diffusion matrix H records how each source's output spreads. A polluter that affects several points must hold a portfolio of licenses covering all of them. Montgomery showed that both kinds of market allocate licenses efficiently, but pollution-license markets apply more widely.

nature-pol-287.title: Water quality trading: cleaner rivers at the lowest cost
nature-pol-287.text: Different polluters in one watershed, the land draining to a river or lake, face very different costs to control the same pollutant. Water quality trading puts that gap to work. Sources that can cut water pollution cheaply sell pollution-reduction credits to sources for whom cuts are costly. Most programs trade nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen ({{ref:nature-eco-245}}). The US EPA issued its Water Quality Trading Policy in 2003, and all programs must meet the {{ref:nature-pol-155}}. Funders include watershed beneficiaries, polluters compensating for their impacts and public good payers.

nature-pol-284.title: White certificates: trading proof of saved energy
nature-pol-284.text: In some countries, suppliers of electricity, gas and oil must deliver efficiency measures equal to a set percentage of their annual sales, or pay a penalty. White certificates are tradable proof that a certain amount of energy saving has been achieved. They are cousins of green certificates. As with emissions trading, tradability in theory meets the overall saving target at least cost. Great Britain started a scheme in 2002, Italy in 2005, and France and Denmark a year later.

nature-pol-268.title: Carbon retirement: taking permits off the market for good
nature-pol-268.text: A record 164 million credits ({{ref:nature-mkt-081}}) were retired in voluntary markets in 2023. Retirement means permanently removing emission allowances or credits from circulation, so they can never be sold or used again. Under a cap, retiring allowances shrinks supply, which raises their scarcity and price. The EU's Market Stability Reserve invalidated about 2.5 billion allowances on 1 January 2023, and more than 3 billion by 2026. In voluntary markets, companies retire credits to offset emissions they cannot yet eliminate. Citizen groups have even bought and retired sulfur dioxide allowances in US EPA auctions, to cut the supply available to polluters.

nature-pol-280.title: Transferable development rights: paying land to stay open
nature-pol-280.text: Land carries a bundle of {{ref:nature-econ-621}}, including the right to develop it. Transferable development rights let that one right be sold on its own. Developers buy the building rights of land in a protected sending area: farmland, wilderness or historic sites at risk of development. They use those rights to build more densely in a receiving area, an urban place suited to higher density. Landowners get paid for conserving environmental, heritage or farming values, and sprawl is curbed by concentrating development. Such programs operate in over 200 U.S. communities.
